ABSTRACT
Context. RR Lyraes (RRLs) are important tracers of old stellar populations and crucial distance indicators. To complement large
variability surveys such as Gaia and Rubin-LSST, the topology of the RRL instability strip (IS) and their period-luminosity-metallicity
(PLZ) and period-Wesenheit-metallicity (PWZ) relations need to be updated using state-of-the-art stellar evolution and pulsation
models.
Aims. We employ the updated set of BaSTI horizontal-branch (HB) evolutionary models, with finer sampling in effective temperature
and metallicity, and compute the corresponding pulsation models using the mesa-rsp module building on the approach of Marconi et
al. (2015). We aim to quantify how the predicted IS boundaries and PLZ/PWZ relations depend on the adopted convection prescription
and mixing-length parameter.
Methods. We compute a grid of linear non-adiabatic radial pulsation models with mesa-rsp, covering −2.2 ≤[Fe/H] ≤+0.06 dex.
Seven convection configurations are explored including the recently empirically calibrated prescription for RRLs by Kovács et al.
(2024). Analytical IS boundaries are derived for RRab and RRc pulsators and transformed into several photometric systems (Gaia,
OGLE, 2MASS, and LSST) and the Kiel diagram.
Results. The updated evolutionary models do not substantially change the pulsation predictions: RRab IS edges agree well with
previous results, while the RRc red edge is slightly redder. The width of the IS decreases systematically with increasing αMLT, and
RRc is relatively more sensitive to the convection prescription than RRab. Testing both linear and quadratic edge fits, RRc IS favours
a quadratic luminosity term in most cases, indicating intrinsic curvature of the first-overtone IS. The observed sample lies well within
our predicted IS edges when compared in the (J −Ks)0 versus MKs color–magnitude diagram. The PLZ and PWZ relations are also
in good agreement with previous empirical and theoretical calibrations across the NIR bands; however, the convection prescription
giving the closest match is wavelength dependent. The theoretical Gaia PWZ relation shows a modest offset from the empirical Milky
Way field relation, which diminishes significantly when compared at matching cluster metallicities.
Conclusions. The predicted IS boundaries and PLZ/PWZ relations exhibit a coupled dependence on pulsation mode, metallicity, and
convective treatment, with no single prescription performing uniformly best across all observational planes. The theoretical relations
presented here are directly applicable to large RRL datasets from ongoing and forthcoming surveys, including Gaia and Rubin-LSST.

1. Introduction
RR Lyrae stars (RRLs) are low-mass Population II pulsating
variables, with masses of 0.5–0.8 M⊙and periods of ∼0.2–
1.0 days (Smith 1995; Catelan 2009; Marconi et al. 2015; Bhard-
waj 2020; Clementini et al. 2023), occupying the classical in-
stability strip (IS) at the intersection of the horizontal branch
(HB) in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (HRD), (Catelan et al.
2004; Catelan 2009). As tracers of ancient (≳10 Gyr) popu-
lations (Baade 1944; D’Orazi et al. 2025), RRLs are powerful
probes of the assembly history of the Galactic halo, thick disk,
bulge, and dwarf galaxies (e.g., Helmi 2008; Luongo et al. 2024;
Medina et al. 2025a). They are classified by pulsation mode:
fundamental-mode (RRab, P ∼0.29–1.00 d, high-amplitude
asymmetric light curves) and first-overtone (RRc, P ∼0.20–0.51
d, lower-amplitude sinusoidal curves), with double-mode RRd
pulsators oscillating in both modes (Clementini et al. 2023).
RRLs have long been recognized as fundamental distance in-
dicators, owing to the well-established correlation between their
absolute visual magnitude and iron abundance ([Fe/H]) (e.g.,
Catelan et al. 2004; Marconi et al. 2015). Since the pioneer-
ing work of Longmore et al. (1986), their Period-Luminosity
(PL) and Period-Wesenheit (PW) relations in the near-infrared
(NIR), have been extensively investigated and continuously re-
fined through both theoretical modeling and observational stud-
ies. These relations establish RRLs as robust tracers of dis-
tances within the Milky Way and nearby galaxies (Smith 1995;
Catelan & Smith 2015; Bhardwaj et al. 2023, 2024; Ngeow &
Bhardwaj 2026). The advent of large-scale photometric surveys
such as the Gaia mission (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016, 2023)
and the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time

A fundamental concept in the theory of pulsating stars is the
IS, the region in the HRD, where stellar pulsations are excited by
the κ and γ-mechanisms operating in the Hydrogen and partial
Helium ionization zones (Cox 1980; Bono & Stellingwerf 1994).
The location and topology of the RRL IS depend sensitively on
stellar parameters such as mass, luminosity, effective tempera-
ture, and chemical composition, as well as on the treatment of
convection in pulsation models (Di Criscienzo et al. (2004b),
Marconi et al. (2015, hereafter M15)). Precise theoretical pre-
dictions of the IS are essential for interpreting observed RRL
populations and for deriving reliable PL and PW relations. Over
the past decades, significant progress has been made in model-
ing RRL pulsations. Nonlinear convective pulsation models have
provided detailed predictions of light curves, pulsation ampli-
tudes, and IS boundaries (e.g., Bono & Stellingwerf 1994; Kol-
láth et al. 2000, 2002; Szabó et al. 2004; Marconi et al. 2015,
2022). In particular, M15 presented a comprehensive theoretical
framework based on pulsation models coupled with evolutionary
constraints from Bag of Stellar Tracks and Isochrones (BaSTI)
stellar models by Pietrinferni et al. (2006). Their work estab-
lished widely used relations for the IS boundaries and provided
a theoretical basis for interpreting RRL observations across a
range of metallicities (0.0001 < Z < 0.02). Although these mod-
els have successfully reproduced many observed properties of
RRLs, they were constructed using earlier generations of evolu-
tionary calculations and a particular set of convection parame-
ters. Recent advances in stellar evolution modeling (Pietrinferni
et al. 2021) and alternative treatments of convection in mesa-rsp
provide the possibility to reassess and further improve these pre-
dictions.
Recent advances in stellar evolutionary calculations have
led to updated predictions for HB stars (Hidalgo et al. 2018;
Pietrinferni et al. 2021). In particular, the revised BaSTI database
incorporates improved input physics, including updated solar
metal mixtures, electron conduction opacities, and nuclear re-
action rates, leading to revisions in the predicted properties of
HB stars (for more detail see Sect. 2.1). While these updates are
generally expected to preserve the overall agreement with pre-
vious calculations, they may introduce modest changes in the
mass–luminosity distribution and, consequently, small but po-
tentially relevant shifts in the predicted location of the RRL IS.
Consequently, the theoretical relations should be reexamined in
light of these updated evolutionary models.
Another important aspect that remains insufficiently ex-
plored is the sensitivity of the IS boundaries to the adopted con-
vection parameters. Convection strongly influences the red edge
of the IS, and uncertainties in convection modeling represent
a major source of theoretical error in pulsation models (e.g.,
Stellingwerf 1982; Bono & Stellingwerf 1994; Kovács et al.
2023; Deka et al. 2024, 2026). For example Di Criscienzo et al.
(2004b,a) showed that a higher value of the mixing length pa-
rameter is required to fit the position of the RRL IS red edge than
for the blue edge and that adopting a fixed value for the whole
IS might introduce errors. Moreover, the model fitting of multi-
band light curves (see e.g. Marconi & Clementini 2005; Marconi
& Degl’Innocenti 2007) suggests that higher mixing length val-
ues are required to fit the pulsation amplitude and morphology
of RRcs than RRabs. Recently, Kovács et al. (2023, 2024) per-
formed a detailed calibration of turbulent convection (TC) pa-
rameters for RRLs in the globular cluster M3, using both radial
velocity (RV) and V-band light curves. However, this calibration
was limited to narrow period ranges; 0.50 −0.71 days for RRab
and 0.29 −0.34 days for RRc, so its applicability across the full
RRL population has yet to be tested. While Kovács et al. (2023,
2024) provided distinct sets of TC parameters for RRab and RRc
stars (optimized separately for the Budapest-Florida and the Ra-
dial Stellar Pulsation (RSP) module of the Modules for Exper-
iments in Stellar Astrophysics (mesa; Paxton et al. 2010, 2013,
2015, 2018, 2019; Jermyn et al. 2023) codes) and successfully
reproduced the observed RV curves, notable discrepancies re-
main in the modeled light curves. Additional observational con-
straints have recently been provided by Cruz Reyes et al. (2024),
who compiled a large catalog of RRLs in Galactic globular clus-
ters using Gaia DR3 and derived empirical IS boundaries. When
compared with theoretical predictions based on mesa models,
their analysis suggested that different helium abundances were
required to reproduce the observed locations of RRab and RRc
stars within the IS. However, since these theoretical boundaries
were derived using a single set of TC parameters, the extent to
which uncertainties in convection modeling may contribute to
the observed discrepancies remains unclear (see for example De
Somma et al. 2022; Deka et al. 2024). A systematic investiga-
tion of the effects of different mixing-length values, convection
parameter sets, as well as chemical composition, is therefore es-
sential to assess the robustness of theoretical IS predictions. Fur-
thermore, modern photometric surveys operate in specific pho-
tometric systems, such as those of Gaia, LSST, Roman, and the
James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). This requires theoretical
predictions to be expressed directly in the corresponding obser-
vational planes, rather than solely in the HRD or traditional op-
tical bands.
In this work, we present updated theoretical predictions for
the RRL IS based on a new grid of pulsation models computed
with the mesa-rsp module and evolutionary constraints from up-
dated BaSTI HB models. Our model grid spans a range of metal-
licities extending to slightly more metal-rich regimes than those
considered by M15. We also explore two TC parameter sets
in the mesa-rsp. In addition, we explore the impact of differ-
ent mixing-length values on the location of the IS boundaries
and quantify the resulting shifts in effective temperature. Finally,
we derive the predicted IS edges into the Optical Gravitational
Lensing Experiment (OGLE), Gaia, Two Micron All Sky Sur-
vey (2MASS) and LSST photometric systems, providing rela-
tions that can be directly compared with the observations.
This paper is organised as follows. Sect. 2.1 describes the
BaSTI evolutionary models. Sect. 2.2–2.3 present the mesa-rsp
pulsation models, the model grid, the convection parameter sets,
and the model selection criteria. Sect. 3 analyses the IS topology
and its dependence on metallicity and convection prescription
across multiple photometric systems, and presents comparisons
with previous theoretical work and observational data. Section 4
discusses the implications, caveats, and limitations of the present
work. Sect. 5 summarises the main conclusions.

The numerical setup follows our previous implementation
in Deka et al. (2024), based on the fiducial values in Paxton
et al. (2019), with the main adopted parameters summarized
here. Calculations were performed with mesa-rsp, which solves
the time-dependent pulsation equations on a Lagrangian mesh
partitioned into inner and outer regions by an anchor temper-
ature, Tanchor = 11, 000 K for all models. Our standard setup
employed Ntotal = 200 mass zones, of which Nouter = 60 were lo-
cated above the anchor layer. Where this zoning did not yield a
stable initial hydrostatic model, we adopted a reduced mesh with
Ntotal = 150 and Nouter = 40. The remaining numerical controls,
including the inner boundary temperature Tinner = 2 × 106 K,
followed the recommendations of Paxton et al. (2019); see also
Appendix B of Deka et al. (2024) for details. These numerical
parameters were kept fixed throughout the full model grid.
mesa-rsp adopts the time-dependent TC formalism of Kuh-
fuss (1986), as implemented by Smolec & Moskalik (2008). This
prescription contains eight dimensionless parameters regulating
mixing length, eddy viscosity, turbulent driving and dissipation,
convective transport, turbulent pressure, turbulent flux, and ra-
diative losses. Paxton et al. (2019) provides four combinations
of these parameters, labeled A, B, C, and D, differing in the
inclusion of radiative cooling, turbulent pressure, and turbulent
flux. In Set A, turbulent pressure, turbulent flux, and radiative
cooling are neglected, and the static limit of the Kuhfuss for-
malism becomes locally equivalent to standard mixing-length
theory. Set B includes radiative cooling following Wuchterl &
Feuchtinger (1998). Set C includes turbulent pressure and tur-
bulent flux, following Yecko et al. (1998). Set D includes all
these effects simultaneously. These parameters remain uncali-
brated with observations; preliminary attempts to constrain them
empirically for RRLs and classical Cepheids exist, but only for
relatively small samples, so a generally applicable calibration is
still lacking (e.g., Kovács et al. 2023, 2024; Deka et al. 2026).
The systematic exploration of these parameters within mesa-rsp
is important, but a full exploration is computationally very ex-
pensive. We therefore adopt the fiducial convection sets from
Paxton et al. (2019) as a physically motivated starting point, se-
lecting Set A and Set D as representative of the simplest and
most complex prescriptions, supplemented by the empirically
calibrated K24 set which, to our knowledge, has not previously
been investigated for the RRL IS. For set A and D, we consider
three mixing-length values, αMLT = 1.2, 1.5, and 1.8, chosen to
bracket the range of convective efficiencies reported in the liter-
ature depending on pulsation mode, metallicity, and photometric
band (e.g., Di Criscienzo et al. 2004b; Netzel et al. 2023). How-
ever, for K24 set, we use αMLT = 1.5 as reported in K24. We
caution that the optimal αMLT depends on the specific convec-
tion formulation, so values from different codes or TC schemes
are not directly comparable.
2.3. Determination of pulsational stability
For each equilibrium model in the input grid, we performed a
LNA stability analysis of the first ten radial eigenmodes. Here,
however, we restrict the discussion to the two modes relevant for
RRL pulsation: the FU (RRab) and FO (RRc) modes. The stabil-
ity of a given mode was determined from its linear growth rate,
obtained from the complex eigenfrequency in the nonadiabatic
calculation. Modes with positive growth rates were classified as
linearly unstable (excited), those with negative growth rates as
linearly stable (damped). At high effective temperatures, mod-
els are stable due to insufficient driving in the partial ionization
zones. As effective temperature decreases, the growth rate be-
comes positive, indicating the onset of pulsational instability; at
lower temperatures, increased convective efficiency suppresses
pulsations and the growth rate turns negative again. This behav-
ior defines the blue and red IS edges. Including convection in the
linear mode of mesa-rsp enables prediction of both edges.
For each adopted luminosity level, the blue and red IS edges
were identified from the bluest and reddest effective tempera-
tures, respectively, at which the mode changes from stable to
unstable. The edge temperatures derived at different luminosity
levels were then fitted separately with linear relations for the blue
and red boundaries. The resulting IS boundaries and their depen-
dence on metallicity and convective parameters are discussed in
the following sections.

3.1.3. Comparison with Marconi et al. (2015)
We compare our IS boundaries with the theoretical predictions
of M15, the most comprehensive previous RRL IS study based
on nonlinear convective pulsation models (αMLT = 1.5); whereas
our predictions are derived from linear pulsation models. The
comparison is shown in Fig. B.3 at four representative metal-
licities, for the intermediate value αMLT = 1.5; the quantitative
analysis below extends to all three αMLT values we explored.
The overall IS topology is qualitatively consistent between
the two studies. Both predict the IS shifting to cooler temper-
atures and lower luminosities with increasing metallicity, with
comparable luminosity slopes (|β| ≈0.03–0.10) and metallicity
coefficients of similar sign and magnitude — these global trends
are therefore robust to the choice of pulsation code.
The primary systematic difference is a zero-point offset in
Teff. For the blue edge, all our model sets predict cooler temper-
atures than M15 by ≈10–110 K, with the offset increasing with
αMLT in Set D but decreasing in Set A. Notably, at αMLT = 1.5
the Set A blue edge (∆log Teff = −0.0049, ≈−34 K) and the
RRc Set A blue edge (∆log Teff ≈0 K) agree excellently with
M15, making Set A at αMLT = 1.5 the closest match to the
Stellingwerf-code predictions for the blue boundary.
The red edge reveals a more physically significant trend. In
Set A, the offset relative to M15 increases monotonically with
αMLT: at αMLT = 1.2 the RRab red edge lies ≈47 K cooler than
M15, whereas at 1.8 it lies ≈+172 K hotter. This sign reversal
as convective efficiency increases directly reflects more efficient
convective quenching of pulsation driving at higher αMLT, which
pushes the red edge to higher temperatures. The same reversal
occurs in Set D but at smaller amplitude, with the RRab red edge
crossing the M15 value between αMLT = 1.5 and 1.8. The K24
prescription, with a mean red edge offset of only ≈−9 K, is
closest to the M15 red edge.
For RRc, the red edge is systematically hotter than M15
across all sets and αMLT values, with offsets ranging from ≈
+26 K (Set D, αMLT = 1.2) to ≈+353 K (Set A, αMLT = 1.8).
This offset grows strongly with αMLT in both sets, making the red
edge the IS boundary most sensitive to convection prescription.
Furthermore, across all metallicities the Set A red edge offset in-
creases steadily toward higher Z (from ≈+44 K at Z = 0.000199
to ≈+113 K at Z = 0.015070), while the blue-edge offset re-
mains broadly constant.
These results, obtained within the framework of linear pulsa-
tion analysis, show that convection prescription introduces sys-
tematic IS boundary uncertainties of order ∼100–350 K. Build-
ing on M15, this work extends that framework by exploring three
prescriptions at three αMLT values each, providing a quantitative
mapping of this uncertainty space over the full metallicity range
of observed RRL populations, including metallicities up to ap-
proximately solar or slightly super-solar values (+0.06 dex) —
not covered in Marconi et al. (2015) but covered in Bono et al.
(1997a). We return to the PLZ/PWZ comparison with Marconi
et al. (2021) and Marconi et al. (2022) in the following sections.

originate from the updated BaSTI ZAHB or from the pulsa-

ZAHB models adopted for the mesa-rsp grid, at two representa-

in Fig. B.4. Relative to the previous BaSTI release used by

the optical and NIR versions as arising from the same mecha-

and hence opacity and convective efficiency – produces earlier
quenching. The reversal’s greater systematicity and significance

models.

3.3. The Kiel Diagram
Large-scale spectroscopic surveys are now delivering atmo-
spheric parameters (Teff, log g, [Fe/H]) for thousands of RRL.
Wang et al. (2024) derived parameters for ∼11 000 RRLs
from LAMOST spectra, and the DESI Year 1 catalog (Med-
ina et al. 2025b) has provided the first empirical constraints on
the metallicity-dependent topology of the RRL IS using phase-
corrected effective temperatures for a sample of comparable
size. Upcoming surveys such as 4MOST (de Jong et al. 2019),
WEAVE (Dalton et al. 2012), and SDSS-V (Kollmeier et al.
2017) will push this further by an order of magnitude. In this
context, the Kiel diagram (log Teff vs. log g) represents one of
the most direct planes for comparing theoretical IS boundaries
with spectroscopic observations, as it is entirely independent of
distance, reddening, and photometric calibration. The boundary
relations derived here (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.
20611450) are therefore directly applicable to these datasets
without any intermediate transformation.
For RRab stars, the linear model is preferred for 12 of 14
configurations, with the quadratic term reaching significance
only for the red edge at the highest αMLT in both Set A and Set D.

4. Discussion
The present study is based on LNA pulsation models, computa-
tionally efficient and well suited for predicting IS boundaries and
mean magnitudes across a wide range of chemical compositions
and evolutionary parameters. Stellar evolution inputs play a cru-
cial role in RRL pulsation calculations, since the adopted stellar
mass and ZAHB luminosity for a given metallicity directly set
the period scale and zero-point of the PLZ/PWZ relations (e.g.,
Szabó et al. 2004; Marconi et al. 2015). The primary aim of this
work is to investigate how updated evolutionary physics, specif-
ically the recent BaSTI HB models (Pietrinferni et al. 2021),
propagates into the predicted pulsation properties of RRLs, of-
fering a new theoretical framework for their use as distance and
metallicity indicators.
The predicted IS edges show the expected behaviour: for
both RRab and RRc, the blue and red edges shift redward with
increasing metallicity, regardless of convection parameters, con-
sistent with earlier predictions (Bono & Stellingwerf (1994),
M15). The magnitude of this shift, however, is highly sensitive
to the convection prescription, particularly at the red edge.
An interesting behaviour is seen for the RRc red edge: rather
than shifting monotonically redward with metallicity, it initially
moves redward before turning bluer at higher metallicities. This
non-monotonic trend is a distinctive feature of FO pulsation, ex-
plainable by the confinement of FO pulsation to a more external
envelope region than the FU mode, though it warrants further in-
vestigation with nonlinear models. Furthermore, αMLT = 1.8 ap-
pears too restrictive for RRc pulsators in the metal-rich regime:
for [Fe/H] ≳−0.3 dex, no stable RRc models are found, suggest-
ing this convective efficiency suppresses FO pulsation entirely at
higher metallicities.
We also note that Cruz Reyes et al. (2024) recently com-
piled a catalogue of 2824 RRL stars in 115 Galactic globular
clusters using Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry, comparing
observed IS boundaries with mesa-rsp models at fixed convec-
tion parameters while varying helium abundance. They found
Y = 0.290 broadly reproduces the observed IS for both modes,
but a higher value (Y = 0.357) is required for RRc stars, while a
lower value (Y = 0.220) is favoured for RRab, suggesting mode-
dependent sensitivity of the inferred IS topology to helium con-
tent. Here, however, we show that variations in metallicity and
convection prescription, together with helium abundance deter-
mined self-consistently via the enrichment ratio ∆Y/∆Z (Pietrin-
ferni et al. 2021), can produce comparable shifts in the predicted
IS boundaries. We emphasise that convection in 1D nonlinear
pulsation models remains necessarily parametrized, and multi-
dimensional radiation-hydrodynamical calculations would ulti-
mately be required to calibrate these prescriptions from first prin-
ciples. Nevertheless, our results demonstrate that the inferred IS
topology is not driven by helium abundance alone: helium con-
tent, metal fraction, and convective efficiency are coupled ingre-
dients whose combined effect must be considered when inter-
preting observed IS morphologies. A self-consistent exploration
of this multidimensional parameter space, ideally informed by
future 2D/3D hydrodynamical constraints on convection, repre-
sents a compelling direction for future work.
The formal preference for αMLT = 1.2 in the NIR PLZ/PWZ
metric most plausibly reflects the wider IS produced by less effi-
cient convection: a broader strip increases the model sample size
and extends the period baseline, mechanically improving the re-
gression slope without implying more accurate red-edge predic-
tions. The CMD comparison in Sect. 3.4 offers an independent
check, showing that αMLT = 1.2 red edges extend into regions of
the observational plane essentially unpopulated by the data. This
underscores the value of combining multiple diagnostics — IS
boundaries, PLZ/PWZ coefficients, and light curve morphology
— rather than relying on any single metric.
The K24 prescription gives the best match in the Ks and
WH,Ks bands for both RRab and the combined sample, notable
given this set is empirically calibrated against observed RRL
light curves. Two caveats apply, however. First, K24 provides
separate parameters for RRab and RRc, whereas we adopt their
recommended global RRL set uniformly across both modes
for computational convenience; the mode-specific calibrations
may improve agreement further, particularly for RRc. Second,

5. Summary and Conclusions
We presented linear pulsation model predictions for RRL stars
based on updated BaSTI HB evolutionary tracks and the mesa-
rsp module, focusing on IS topology for both FU and FO modes
across seven convection sets. The IS boundaries were trans-
formed into multiple observational photometric systems for di-
rect comparison with current and forthcoming surveys, includ-
ing Gaia, OGLE, 2MASS, LSST, and the Kiel diagram. PLZ
and PWZ relations were derived in the near-infrared JHKs bands
and in the Gaia bands. The NIR relations were compared against
the empirical relations of Bhardwaj et al. (2023) for RRab and
combined samples, and M15 for RRc stars, while the Gaia PWZ
relation was compared against Marconi et al. (2021) and Garo-
falo et al. (2022). The main findings are summarised as follows:
– IS topology and analytical relations: We derived analyti-
cal relations for the blue and red IS boundaries as a function
of luminosity and metallicity, in linear and quadratic forms,
for both modes across all seven sets. The quadratic term is
warranted far more often for RRc than RRab, particularly at
the red edge, indicating intrinsic curvature of the FO IS with
luminosity across all planes examined. The metallicity co-
efficient γ is consistently negative at the blue edge for both
modes, confirming the hot boundary shifts to cooler temper-
atures at higher Z.
– Effect of convection prescription and αMLT: IS width de-
creases systematically with increasing αMLT for both modes
and all sets, consistent with previous nonlinear analyses.
Set D produces broader strips than Set A at fixed αMLT,
driven by a redward displacement of the red edge; K24 falls
consistently between the two. RRc is substantially more sen-
sitive to convection prescription than RRab, with width dif-
ferences up to ∼280 K between Set A and Set D at αMLT =
1.5.
– Comparison with M15: The global IS topology is qualita-
tively consistent with M15, with comparable luminosity and
metallicity coefficients. The main difference is a Teff zero-
point offset of ∼100–350 K in the red edge, depending on
mode, convection set, and αMLT; the blue edge offset is
small in all cases. At αMLT = 1.5, Set A best matches the
M15 RRc red edge, while Set D best matches the RRab red
edge.
– IS boundaries in observational planes: We provide IS
boundary relations in Johnson-Cousins (V−I, I), Gaia (GBP−
GRP,G), LSST (g −r, g) and (g −i, g), 2MASS (J −Ks, Ks),
and Kiel (log Teff–log g) planes. Patterns from the L–Teff
plane — quadratic RRc boundaries and the negative metal-
licity dependence of the RRc red edge at high convective ef-
ficiency recur across all systems. However, the NIR reversal
of the RRc red-edge metallicity coefficient is more system-
atic and significant than in the optical.
– CMD comparison: In (J−Ks)0 vs. MKs, Set D at αMLT = 1.2
overestimates IS width, while Set A and Set D at αMLT =
1.8 and K24 marginally underestimate it. Set A and Set D at
αMLT = 1.5 best match the observed red-edge locus for both
modes.
– PLZ and PWZ relations in NIR: Formally, Set D at αMLT =
1.2 minimizes the normalised distance to Bhardwaj et al.
(2023) in most bands; however, it also produces the widest
IS, which may artificially extend the model period baseline.
Among prescriptions consistent with the observed IS width
(αMLT ≥1.5), Set D at αMLT = 1.5 is most competitive for
RRab. K24 performs competitively in Ks and WH,Ks. No sin-
gle prescription matches best across all bands, suggesting a
wavelength dependence of the preferred parameters.
– PWZ relations in Gaia: The global Gaia PWZ fit agrees
well with Marconi et al. (2021) across the full period range,
but shows a systematic offset from the empirical relation
of Garofalo et al. (2022), attributed to the latter’s broader,
more metal-poor calibration baseline. Agreement improves
substantially against individual globular clusters with metal-
licities close to our grid, with Set A at αMLT = 1.5 most
consistent. As in the NIR, convection prescription introduces
greater dispersion in the RRc relation than the RRab, where
all prescriptions remain tightly clustered.
This paper is the first in a series on a comprehensive the-
oretical characterization of RRL pulsation properties using up-
dated BaSTI evolutionary inputs and mesa-rsp. The grid extends
to near-solar and mildly super-solar metallicities ([Fe/H] up to
+0.06 dex), extending the theoretical IS framework of M15 for
comparison with modern surveys sampling RRL stars across
a broad metallicity baseline. A natural next step is a comple-
mentary grid of nonlinear convective models using the same
BaSTI inputs, enabling direct comparison with observed pul-
sation amplitudes and light curve morphology across the full
metallicity range, and providing tighter constraints on the pre-
ferred convection prescription and a more definitive assessment
of the wavelength-dependent behaviour identified here. Ongo-
ing and forthcoming surveys, including Gaia DR4, LSST, Ro-
man, and 4MOST, will substantially increase the number of RRL
